claim: The lane lets two heavy commands run at once, not one: research-tree/lane/capacity.txt held 2 when read on 2026-11-18 (lane.mjs default 1, at most 4); the protocol says 2 since 03:50 on 2026-11-17 and that the log shows commands overlapping, while the briefs say one at a time.

Of the bottleneck signals the literature uses, this PC already logs three: free memory (Available MBytes) and whole-PC processor % every 2 s (research-tree/tools/recorder.ps1) and each heavy command's queue wait (waited_ms in the lane log); nothing logs the processor queue length, per-process memory, page-ins or conflicts between agents.

Suleman, Qureshi and Patt 2008 (ASPLOS, 32-core simulator, one program at a time): when every thread must pass a critical section, so its total time grows linearly with the thread count, the best count is sqrt(T_NoCS / T_CS) from a short one-thread training run, capped at the cores; on 4 synchronisation-limited programs it was within 1 % of the best fixed count.
note: Checked by grep in the paper text: lines 30, 210, 251, 256, 260 of the collector's raw.txt. The square root needs the serial work to grow with the worker count.

claim: Suleman and others 2008: with a serial step and a bandwidth limit, running at min(P_CS, P_BW, cores) is proved best in their model; over 12 programs it cut average time by 17 % against one thread per core (32), not against the best fixed count, and programs limited by neither kept all 32 threads.
note: Paper text lines 626, 631, 634 and the Appendix (693-712). The proof covers the two-limit model only.

claim: Suleman and others 2008: a bandwidth-limited program saturates the bus at P_BW = 100 / BU1 threads (BU1 = bus busy % with one thread, from a hardware counter), within 3 % of the best count on 4 programs; it assumes bus use grows linearly with threads and picked 7 where 8 was best.

Johnson and others 2010 (ASPLOS, 64-context Niagara II): one sensor, runnable threads in excess of hardware contexts, used to make spinning threads sleep, kept 85 % of peak throughput at 200 % load, where plain spinning past 100 % wastes up to 85 % of processor time; it oscillates when load spikes are short against its update interval.
note: Paper text lines 72, 103, 128, 231, 472. The threads it sheds are spinners, which cost nothing to stop.

claim: Denning 1968: a process should be active only if its working set fits in main memory, and in his model one program too many causes a complete collapse of service; this is analytic, with no measured gain.
note: Paper text p2 lines 73, 220; p1 lines 642, 679. Windows "working set" is resident memory, not Denning's recently used set.

claim: Schroeder and others 2006 (ICDE, 17 setups on two databases): the number of jobs at once needed for near-best throughput follows the number of resources the work keeps busy, hardly whether it is CPU-, I/O- or lock-bound, and was under 20 in every setup; their feedback loop needed about 100 transactions per observation and converged in under 10 steps.
note: Paper text lines 278, 353, 356, 505-507. For response time the level is set by job-size variability instead (line 352).

claim: Controllers that search on throughput need many finished units per step and one peak: Heiss and Wagner 1991 (simulation) want rather hundreds of departures than some tens per interval and assume the only local maximum is global; Cicada 2017 found one peak in its workloads.
note: Heiss-Wagner text is OCR ("dcparturcs", line 130); their gain is in figures not read.

claim: Queueing delay, not processor utilisation, is the overload signal in DAGOR 2018 (high CPU is not overload while queuing time stays low) and Breakwater 2020 (queue length is a poor indicator when service times vary); Ousterhout 2015 found CPU near 100 % with disks at most 25 % busy, and removing disk waits cut job time by at most 19 % (median).

Lazowska and others 1984 (QSP ch. 3 and 5): utilisation equals throughput times demand, the centre with the largest demand is the bottleneck and caps throughput, and improving any other centre is futile at heavy load; the bounds rest on one assumption, that a unit's demand does not depend on how many others are present.
note: The assumption fails under paging and lock convoys; N* is where the light- and heavy-load bounds meet (the formula is garbled in the scan).

claim: Wang and Kimura 2016 (MOCC, 288 cores): a page switches from optimistic reads to read locks once its abort counter reaches a threshold (recommended 5 to 10, a logarithmic counter, so about 2^H aborts), 8 and 23 times faster than pure optimistic and pure locking at high conflict and identical to optimistic on TPC-C; counters are reset periodically.

Moenkeberg and Weikum 1992 (12-processor Sequent, one Swiss bank trace, page locks): holding new transactions while the conflict ratio (locks held by all over locks held by unblocked transactions) exceeds 1.3 gave 1.5 times better mean and 1.8 times better 90th-percentile response time than the best fixed level; Thomasian 1998 puts the ratio at 1.25 to 1.43 (1.26 to 1.60 for mixes) with no guarantee elsewhere.

Lim and Agarwal 1994 (Alewife simulator and 16-node machine): switching protocol on a contention threshold, and back only after a run of quiet acquisitions, came close to the best fixed protocol at all contention levels with modest gains for locks, degraded once contention flipped about every 1,000 critical sections, and stayed better than the worst fixed protocol.
note: Paper text lines 8, 222, 246, 254-258, 761. The threshold is tuned per machine.

claim: Marathe, Scherer and Scott 2005 (16-processor SunFire, Java STM): adaptive eager or lazy acquire matched the best fixed system in all scenarios tested, but in most cases neither method was dramatically better; the one large gap was over 5 times on one benchmark, and thresholds (writes 25 %, early releases 50 %) were largely insensitive.

Breakwater 2020 raises admitted work additively and cuts it multiplicatively on measured queueing delay, at about 5 % overhead at capacity and 5.7 % more goodput than SEDA at twice capacity; DAGOR 2018 uses a 20 ms average queuing time refreshed every second or 2,000 requests; both are tuned for requests of microseconds to milliseconds.

Ousterhout and others 2017 (Monotasks, Spark on 20 machines): with work cut into single-resource pieces, a stage's bottleneck is the resource with the largest ideal time, it can differ from stage to stage, and per-resource queues of capacity plus one gave 30 % shorter jobs than hand-set resource use; workloads were chosen with no dominant resource.

Switching cost: CormCC 2018's mediated switch kept at least 93 % of OCC or 2PL throughput and dropped at most about 20 % (PartCC to OCC with long transactions) while stop-all waits for long transactions; Polyjuice 2021 switches in about 3 s without loss but trains for several hundred seconds, so not for changes faster than every few minutes.

Diao and others 2002 (one Apache server): a two-input, two-output controller of CPU and memory utilisation showed a pair of targets can be jointly unreachable ((0.8, 0.4) was infeasible) and that high gains cause limit cycles; its results are qualitative in the text read.

Anselmi and Cremonesi 2010 (analytic, product-form networks, large populations): the bottleneck migrates across stations with the mix of job classes, and a linear program lists which stations can saturate alone or together; no live measurement.

Of the 32 papers the o1 collectors read in full, none switches method by which of several resources is the bottleneck on a live machine with a measured gain, none has a serial step shared by separate programs, and none has work units minutes long with a handful of workers; each result is one form on one benchmark family.
note: Rests on the collectors' gap sections, not on this writer reading every paper; figures were not read in any paper.

claim: proposed correction of r57-0104: it says the lane has capacity 1, but research-tree/lane/capacity.txt holds 2, since 03:50 on 2026-11-17 by the protocol, so part of the 778 logged commands ran with two slots.

The eight claims a choice of bottleneck rule would rest on (o1-claims.md C1 to C8: Suleman's widths and their minimum, Schroeder's level, Denning's memory collapse, wait time over processor use, Johnson's load control, MOCC's threshold, Lim's switching cost) went through one refute round by a fresh Opus reader with the paper texts: all eight PARTIALLY, none confirmed in full, none refuted. Each holds only under its paper's conditions, listed in o1-refute.md.

Cho and others, Protego (NSDI 2023): when requests contend for locks, overload control on queueing delay or processor use fails; it is 'difficult to prevent contention through overload control using traditional signals such as queueing delay and CPU utilization' (l.21), and on Lucene 'Breakwater's admission control and AQM are never triggered, leading to congestion collapse' (l.540). Protego admits work by marginal throughput gain instead. So a shared lock or serial step needs its own signal.
